title: Marketing manager

manager.name: Dana
manager.title: Founder
manager.persona_note: Dana hopes one hire can solve a lot at once. A good recruiter helps narrow it to the two things that matter most.

teaser: Dana founded an accounting software company and wants one marketer who can do it all.
context: The company sells accounting software to small businesses and has about 40 people.
This is the only marketing job. They'll report to Dana.
message: Hi! I need a marketing manager. We're a small team, so they'll be our only marketer, and there's a lot I'd love them to take on.
The job ad lists everything I could think of.
Do you have ten minutes to go over what we need?
ad: Expert in ads, social media, email, events, video and design
framing: Kickoff calls are often short, and hiring managers have a lot on their plate. Dana will share a few first thoughts about the role. Good questions help you both get it right.
end_early: Sorry, I've got to run. Send me what you've got.

needs.n1: Someone to get more businesses asking for a demo, mostly through email and search.
needs.n2: Someone to build the brand with videos.
needs.n3: Someone to run events and trade shows.

beats.label: The wish list
beats.sam: I need someone who can do it all. Ads, social media, email, events, video and design.

choices.text: If they could only do two of those really well, which two would make the biggest difference?
choices.reply: Getting people to book a demo. That's what pays the bills.
choices.why: Asking for the top two helps a long wish list turn into a real job.

choices.text: That's a big range of skills. Should I look for a true all-rounder who has done a bit of everything?
choices.why: Agreeing makes the search almost impossible. Very few people are strong at all of it.

choices.text: Isn't that more than one person can realistically do?
choices.reply: Then I'll find someone who can.
choices.why: Even if it's true, saying it this way makes the founder defend the list instead of trimming it.

choices.text: Where do most of your demo requests come from today?
choices.reply: Our emails and people searching online. Almost none come from social media.
choices.why: A follow-up on what already works shows where the new hire should focus.

choices.text: Social media must be your biggest channel, right?
choices.why: A leading guess was wrong. An open question would have found the facts.

choices.text: Have you been tracking where demos come from?
choices.why: It sounds like you're testing them, and the founder gets defensive instead of sharing what they know.

beats.label: The must-have
beats.sam: They must be a video expert. It's in the ad.

choices.text: How much video are you making today?
choices.reply: Almost none. It just sounded modern when I wrote the ad.
choices.why: Checking a must-have against what happens today often shows it's a wish, not a need.

choices.text: Should I put video at the top of the list, since it's so popular right now?
choices.why: It sounds current, but you'd be chasing a skill the job doesn't use.

choices.text: So video is the top priority for this hire?
choices.why: A leading question turned a loose wish into a firm priority, and now it will shape the whole search.

beats.label: Industry knowledge
beats.sam: They need to understand accounting. Our buyers are accountants.

choices.text: What would they need to explain to buyers, in plain words?
choices.reply: How we save them time at tax season. Our team can teach the rest.
choices.why: Asking how knowledge gets used narrows a big requirement down to a small one.

choices.text: Should I make an accounting background a requirement?
choices.why: That adds another hard filter to an already long list, and makes the search even harder to fill.

choices.text: Is it really necessary for a marketer to understand accounting when your team can explain the product?
choices.why: Challenging the requirement directly starts a debate. Asking how the knowledge gets used would have narrowed it down calmly.

beats.label: Results
beats.sam: I want to see results in the first month.

choices.text: A clear plan in the first month makes sense. What result would matter most by month six?
choices.why: Agreeing on a fair early goal, then asking about six months, sets a target the new hire can actually hit.

choices.text: What kind of results are you hoping for?
choices.why: A good question, but you let an unrealistic timeline stand, and the new hire will feel it.

choices.text: So I can set expectations, is it okay if I tell candidates you're expecting clear results within their first month?
choices.why: Going along with it sets the new hire up to struggle, and strong candidates will notice.

beats.label: The pay
beats.sam: The budget is tight, so let's keep the pay sensible.

choices.text: So I only bring people you can afford, what range has been approved?
choices.why: Tying the question to their goal makes the number easy to share.

choices.text: A tight budget can make an all-rounder hard to find. What number are we actually working with?
choices.why: It's a fair point, and you got the number, but it cost goodwill.

choices.text: Should I aim for the lower end of the market, then?
choices.why: Without a range, you can't tell who's affordable, and aiming low may lose the right person.

beats.note: Since January 2026, many Ontario employers must include the expected pay or a pay range in public job postings.

beats.label: Office days
beats.sam: It's three days a week in the office.

choices.text: That's fair for a small team. So I can describe the role well, what usually happens on those days?
choices.reply: We plan campaigns together, and I work closely with marketing. Ideas move fast when we're in one room.
choices.why: Accepting a reasonable request, then asking what happens on those days, shows curiosity and gives you a real selling point for candidates.

choices.text: Is that firm, or is there some flexibility?
choices.why: It's a fair question, but asked before you understand why those days matter, it can sound like you're already negotiating against the manager.

choices.text: Most marketers I talk to want to work from anywhere. Could we drop the office days?
choices.why: Pushing to change a settled decision, with nothing to back it up, spends goodwill you'll need for the questions that actually change the search.

beats.label: Selling the role
beats.sam: Marketing is mostly just posting things online, really.

choices.text: What would make a great marketer choose this job?
choices.reply: They'd build our marketing from scratch and see their work bring in customers.
choices.why: Asking what makes the job attractive gives you the story for the right candidates.

choices.text: So I should keep the description fairly simple?
choices.why: That makes the job sound small, which puts off the strongest people.

choices.text: Isn't there a lot more to good marketing than posting things online?
choices.why: Questioning the founder's view rarely changes it. A question about the job does.

candidates.name: Ellis
candidates.job: Marketing manager at a payroll software company
facts: Doubled demo requests in a year
Built the email program from scratch

reason.n1: Doubled demo requests through email and search, which is exactly where Dana's customers come from, and it fits the range.

view.n1: Ellis is the person who fills our calendar with demos.

candidates.name: Corin
candidates.job: Marketing manager at a software company
facts: Tripled website visits in a year
Reports on traffic growth to leadership

reason.n1: Strong in the right channels, but focused on website visits. Dana's goal is twice as many demo requests.

view.n1: Corin brings visitors. I need demos.

candidates.name: Shea
facts: Grew a video channel to 50,000 followers

reason.n1: Video matches the old ad, but Dana confirmed they barely use it.

view.n1: Shea's amazing, but that's not what brings in our customers.

candidates.name: Juno
candidates.job: Head of brand at a well-known app
facts: Won an award for a campaign that went viral
Led a rebrand for a company of 500 people

reason.n1: The most impressive resume, but built on social media and brand. Dana said almost no demo requests come from social media.

view.n1: Juno would make us famous. Our buyers find us through email and search.
